text: I appreciate that the authors have carefully considered the original reviewer comments. I have looked at the revised manuscript and the responses to the concerns that I raised. My concerns have mostly been addressed. I have a couple of further minor comments, outlined below. After addressing these comments, I support publication in Nature Communications.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: Note – the line numbers in the PDF file that I received are not aligned with the text. Line numbers stated below are in the approximate location of the relevant text. Section 2.2: This new section reveals an important result that was not evident in the original submitted manuscript: 10 of the CMIP6 models simulate CRE trends that are not significantly different from the observed CRE trend. My concern is that too much attention in this new section is given to the disagreement between observations and the multi-model mean. The reader should not necessarily expect observations to agree with the multi-model mean. The ensemble provides a statistical distribution. Observations can be considered one sample from the distribution. There may be cause for concern if the observations fall far outside the distribution, but apparently that’s not the case. I recommend some careful rewording of this section to guide the reader’s interpretation for comparing observations to the multi-model mean and the ensemble spread.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: L679-686: The W/m2/decade values reported for CO2 increase at Mauna Loa and for the CRE in the North Atlantic and Northeast Pacific could be misleading. These numbers are presented such that the reader is encouraged to make a direct comparison. However, CO2 is a well-mixed greenhouse gas and so is increasing everywhere. In contrast, CRE trends are highly region specific, which is clear in Fig. S7A. Despite having the same units, the representative areas of these values (the “/m2”) are very different. What the authors wrote is technically correct, but I think many readers will get the wrong message. I suggest adding a caveat to the text clarifying that the representative areas of these values reported in W/m2/decade from CO2 and CRE is very different and should not be misinterpreted as a global comparison.

text: This paper proposes a deep learning method that takes the satellite imagery as inputs and generates the human mobility OD flows. The idea is novel since no previous studies have tried OD flow generation by using satellite imagery. However, I have the following concerns about this manuscript.

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: 1. About the rationale and the motivation. The authors’ motivation to do such OD flow generation is that “origin-destination (OD) mobility flow information between different sub-regions of cities that relies on traditional surveys is costly and time- consuming to get updated”. However, the used ground-truth OD flow is the 2020 Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES)[50] dataset in each MSA. In other words, we already have the OD flow data, the proposed method is only to reproduce the existing dataset, which is somehow not that meaningful to me.

text: In this manuscript, the authors proposed Imagery2Flow, a methodology that leverages satellite imagery to predict commute flows. Visual representations derived from satellite imagery are used to extract geospatial features, which are subsequently integrated into a Graph Attention Network to effectively model and predict commute flows. The proposed approach is validated using commute flow data from the top 10 largest Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) in the United States.

text: I have completed the review of the manuscript titled "Global Floating Algae Are Rising," submitted for consideration in Nature Communications. This study presents a novel global analysis of floating algae (FA), using an extensive dataset of satellite imagery over a 20-year period. Including different species and associated environmental factors enhances its originality and significance. While the study contributes valuable insights into FA dynamics, certain issues must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication. Below, I provide a detailed review of the article.

cluster: Machine learning, model performance, and generalization
text: 1. The study employs a deep-learning model (ResUNet) for FA detection but does not provide sufficient details about the training and validation datasets. The accuracy and reliability of a machine learning model depend heavily on the quality and quantity of these datasets. The manuscript states: “The ResUNet deep-learning model is trained and validated using carefully prepared ‘ground truth’ images, with detailed steps described in [48]. For simplicity, such details are not repeated here.” However, reference [48] mentions that the ground-truth images were labeled using a combination of manual outlining and objective delineation.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: Given the vast number of MODIS images analyzed in this study, how was ground-truth data manually determined at such a large scale? Additionally, what quality control measures were implemented to ensure accuracy? The authors should provide a detailed explanation of the ground-truth dataset, including its accuracy, potential biases, and whether any independent validation was performed.

cluster: Machine learning, model performance, and generalization
text: 2. The study employs the ResUNet deep-learning model but does not justify why this model was chosen over more advanced alternatives, such as Vision Transformers (ViT) or other state-of-the-art deep-learning architectures. A comparative analysis of model performance (e.g., accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness) would strengthen the manuscript’s credibility. If ResUNet was selected due to specific advantages, these should be clearly outlined.

text: Global floating algae blooms are expanding Corresponding Author: Professor Chuanmin Hu The scope of the submitted manuscript is to investigate the trend of the abundance and distribution of floating algal scums in the global oceans using satellite observations. The study focuses on both microalgae (phytoplankton) and macroalgae (seaweed). It provides a unique perspective on how the global oceanographic changes affect each species and how some of them are favored compared to others. A deep learning model is utilized to identify floating algal patches, whereas the species level classification is done through a spectral shape algorithm. The manuscript is on high lever, well organized and structured and we believe that will add significant knowledge on the global oceans health.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: What are the noteworthy results? This is a significant and valuable work that pinpoints a global scale implication of shifting climate and oceanographic parameters. The research results indicate that over the last decades, there is a significant and steady increase of both floating microalgae and macroalgae. Furthermore, from 2010 and onward, the rate of the abundance of macroalgae is significantly higher, which indicates that oceanographic parameter changes favor the growth of seaweed and that can lead to a regime shift. These findings identify a global trend and are not limited to a regional scale. Furthermore, the use of satellite data (MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI), ensures that this study can also be replicated in the future years and be directly comparable to these findings.

text: 1) Although the altimetric dataset and methodological developments are undoubtedly valuable, the attribution of observed changes in river water levels (RWL) to climate change over the relatively short period 2016-2024 is methodologically questionable. Climate trends, as defined by the IPCC, require multi-decade observation windows (typically ≥30 years) to distinguish long-term signals from interannual or decadal variability. The focus on extreme events after 2021 (e.g. floods and droughts) is informative but cannot be linked to climate trends. Therefore, many of the reported phrases (‘climate change impacts’ or ‘climate-driven trends’), although plausibly climate-related, should be more cautiously framed as ‘potentially consistent with’ or ‘indicative of’ climate variability, rather than as solid evidence of climate change.

text: Groundwater attribution The assertion that groundwater withdrawal is the primary anthropogenic influence in approximately 37% of deltas relies almost exclusively on GRACE/GRACE-FO trends, which track surface water and groundwater storage. The GRACE mascon footprints, spanning about 300-400 km (approximately 200,000 km²), are significantly larger than most delta plains, often resulting in signal leakage from neighboring aquifers and basins. Given that surface water and groundwater are hydraulically interconnected in many deltas, changes in total water storage also reflect variations in rivers, reservoirs, lakes, and wetlands. Without first subtracting the surface water component (e.g., rivers, wetlands, lakes, and reservoirs) using models that have these components like WGHM or existing in-situ data, and without local well data or pumping records for validation, the connection between the decline in surface water storage plus groundwater storage and aquifer depletion remains speculative. The manuscript should

cluster: Sea level, vertical land motion, InSAR, and coastal elevation change

text: Natural subsidence omitted All deltas experience background “geologic” subsidence: Holocene sediment compaction (typically 1–2 mm yr⁻¹), glacial isostatic adjustment (e.g. ~1 mm yr⁻¹ on the U.S. Gulf Coast), sediment load flexure, and, in some settings, tectonic subsidence. For example, roughly one fifth of the 5 mm yr⁻¹ total subsidence measured in the Mississippi Delta is expected from long term GIA. Excluding such natural terms can inflate the anthropogenic share and misallocate residual variance among groundwater, sediment flux, and urban load. The authors should therefore:

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity

Until this baseline is accounted for, statements that subsidence is “largely human caused” need a caveat: part of the observed sinking would occur even in the absence of contemporary human activity. Addressing these two issues will prevent over interpretation of the anthropogenic contribution and greatly strengthen the manuscript’s validity.

text: The study employs a multilinear regression to associate subsidence rates with three anthropogenic drivers, subsequently using LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) to assess the significance of each driver. With only 40 deltas, any regression or ML model is susceptible to outliers and multicollinearity. The three predictors are likely interrelated— highly urbanized deltas often feature drained wetlands and upstream dams, for instance—resulting in potentially unstable standard coefficients. It is crucial to report variance inflation factors, cross-validated R², and sensitivity to the exclusion of high-leverage deltas. These diagnostics are vital for establishing statistical robustness.

text: The authors of this manuscript present an extensive analysis of elevation changes and their main drivers in selected deltas around the globe. The reveal that approximately 54-65 % of the global deltas are sinking. They analyzed the role of three key anthropogenic drivers and found that groundwater storage loss is the primary driver of elevation changes in 35% of deltas, while groundwater storage, sediment flux decline and urban expansion rather have mixed influences in the other deltas. They show that subsidence is the dominant driver of relative sea level rise in many deltas today, and even under the worst-case, high-emission scenarios (SSP5-8.5), maximum subsidence rates in all deltas will exceed projected sea level rise rates in all deltas. Lastly, the provide a study on the varying adaptation readiness of the selected deltas.

As land subsidence is a process originating in the subsurface, the surface backscatter characteristics do not necessarily change during the subsidence process. On the contrary, sedimentation is a process which alters the surface backscatter characteristics, forcing decorrelation of the InSAR measurements. I’m not challenging your results, I am really interested in these findings. I would be interested to see (1) if you can provide/discuss similar literature which describes the measurement of elevation gain by sedimentation with InSAR, (2) a short analysis whether the InSAR coherence is statistically different in areas which are characterized by elevation gain than in others.

text: This paper identifies a huge number (2.3millions) of deep convective initiation (CI) events over most of Sub-Saharan Africa (with the exception of very wet regions/seasons) and creates composites of Soil Moisture (SM) and rainfall (P) that are stratified by the background directional wind shear.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: i. inhomogeneous SM patterns are associated with the CI events composites for all cases (away from topography) and reach maximum SM dry/wet differences of about 1% (for context most of the CI events, and in particular the extreme ones are occurring in places/seasons when the background SM is of the order of 50%, at least that’s how I see Ex.Fig 2) ii. For optimal SM inhomogeneity, Extreme CI events (whose cloud deepening is characterized by the fastest cooling rates) double (for the highest shear cases) from 3% to 6%, compared to the least favorable SM inhomogeneity (10th to 90th percentile). On average the difference in cooling rate between favorable and unfavorable SM is small for weak shear, but gets to 5-10°C/hr at high shear, equivalent to the effect of doubling CAPE from about 1000 to about 2000J/kg. iii. The precursor warm cloud and the rainfall associated with the composite CI events are placed at the edge of the dry soil patch for most cases, but at the center of the dry patch when the low level and upper level winds have opposite direction. iv. (iii) implies that the spatial correlation between rainfall and soil moisture in a 2°x2° box around the CI is positive for most cases, but negative for the strongest directional shear.

text: COMMENTS TO THE AUTHOR(S) The manuscript “Wind shear enhances soil moisture control on rapid thunderstorm growth” presents a novel, data-rich, and physically consistent analysis of how wind shear modulates the impact of soil moisture heterogeneity on convective initiation (CI) across sub-Saharan Africa. Using an unprecedented dataset (~2.3 million CI events) and integrating high-resolution satellite observations with ERA5 reanalysis and IMERG precipitation products, the authors convincingly show that the most explosive storm initiations preferentially occur over locally dry soils when wind shear is strong. They further demonstrate that the direction of shear determines the sign and magnitude of soil moisture–precipitation (SM–P) feedbacks.

Its implications extend globally, with clear relevance for convective predictability and the evaluation of convection-permitting climate models. The analysis is methodologically rigorous, grounded in theory and observations, and clearly written.

text: This is a review of the manuscript titled, “Wind shear enhances soil moisture control on rapid thunderstorm growth”, submitted to Nature by Taylor et al. The manuscript details the authors’ analysis of vertical (100m- 650 hPa) directional wind shear and convective storm initiation relationships conditioned on mesoscale surface soil moisture gradients. The analysis focuses on sub-Saharan Africa over a 21-year record using: Meteosat Second Generation land surface temperature, cloud top temperature, lighting data; Scatterometer surface soil moisture estimates; NASA IMERG satellite-based precipitation, and ERA5 100m and 650 hPa reanalysis winds. The authors find that the vertical directional wind shear can partly explain the difference in sign and magnitude of previously-reported soil moisture-precipitation correlations that did not consider vertical directional wind shear. In particular, focusing on the most extreme 1% of storms, “…the greatest vertical storm growth occurring where soil moisture-driven circulations oppose the direction of shear-induced cloud displacement. Developing clouds follow the mid-level wind direction, and where this opposes the low-level flow, rainfall is strongly correlated with

The title reference to “rapid thunderstorm growth” is really pointing only to a single subpanel (i.e., Fig 2f) and Extended Fig. 6. The heart of the robust analysis is on convective initiation, not cloud cooling rate. Also, the title states that “wind shear enhances soil moisture influence.” The paper shows that wind shear can “modulate” or “mediate”, but not always “enhance”.

text: With regard to ERA5 winds, the authors wrote in their Response that they were “not aware of any such evaluation [of winds] due to the sparsity of wind observations (even at 10m) across the study area.” Using a dataset of unknown accuracy is a major limitation of this work. Given representativeness of ERA5 low-to-mid level wind shear is central to the authors’ conclusions, they should consider disclosing its accuracy over sub-Saharan Africa is indeed a question mark. One way to do so, is to add a statement to the articles closing paragraph underscoring the need to verify low-level winds upon which the findings depend; improving forecasts of CI location is not only about additional incorporation of land surface state information to forecast systems. I also have a few minor comments:

text: This paper leverages new data from the SWOT mission over a water year to quantify variations in water storage in rivers at a monthly scale. The work also cleverly utilizes these data to detect the shape of river banks and thus the variations in cross section in the active portion of rivers as water level varies. The authors also compare their results with previous storage estimates obtained from modeling.

text: Exciting analysis and paper. This is the type of study I was really looking forward to seeing with SWOT data —the opportunities these data offer for analyzing the global hydrologic cycle are numerous, and this is an exciting first glimpse at what a full water year from SWOT looks like. I very much like the idea behind this paper, as well as the approach and the metrics used to quantify variations in storage in the world’s rivers and the comparison to the modeling study. I also found the concept of tracking water levels from low to high and thus the shape of the active channel particularly exciting. Combined with water extent, water level measurements allow for measurements of river shape from the lowest to the highest water surface elevation detected by SWOT. Super cool.

text: However, I do have a major set of questions related to the SWORD centerlines and the potential impact of their inaccuracies on the study presented. These questions are outlined below:

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: Did you perform any selection of the reaches, or were all SWORD reaches included? From what is written in the paper, it doesn’t seem like a selection was made. I understand there was some filtering based on flags on the water surface elevation, but it’s unclear whether any checks on centerline quality were performed. I ask because I’ve used SWORD extensively and have retraced centerlines in many global river deltas, where SWORD centerlines were often quite inaccurate. I’ve also examined centerlines in other rivers I work on and, in some cases, observed centerlines placed in the floodplain (e.g., the meandering Trinity River has several such reaches).

text: The SWOT satellite is designed to observe Earth’s surface waters and (sub-)mesoscale ocean circulation, employing a novel Ka-band Radar Interferometer for the first time. This paper focuses on mapping riverbank shapes and water storage changes of global rivers using SWOT, which are also the main goals of SWOT. It is interesting to investigate and reveal the river changes and their characteristics in different basin scales and the global scale. Although this study provides the first near-global measurements of active river corridors and river storage variability, I have some suggestions and concerns about SWOT and the results.

text: Lines 480-482. The scientific requirements for river width and WSE from SWOT are 30 m and 0.1 m, respectively. According to the Science Requirements Document, one of SWOT’s requirements is to map rivers wider than 100 m, with an extended goal of 50 m. Have the requirements been validated with other technologies and measurements? Could the uncertainties of these two variables be used to provide uncertainty in storage changes? In the input data provided by the authors, I examined three basins (Amazon, Yangtze, and Ganges) and found that the typical median WSE uncertainty (wse_u) is about 0.4~0.6 m, and ~0.17 m for rivers 50~100 m and >100 m wide. Do these results indicate that SWOT has actually met its stated requirements and goals? If not, does this imply that the estimates for smaller rivers may be inaccurate?

text: Figure 1 presents a highly generalized overview by averaging riverbank shapes along the entire mainstream of major rivers, which masks significant spatial variability. The authors should delve deeper into the data to uncover new geographical patterns or hydrological process insights that are only possible with SWOT's high-resolution observations. For example, an analysis of typical bank morphologies in different geomorphic units or climatic settings and their impact on water storage capacity would more effectively demonstrate the value of this new observational tool. 2---The study's reliance on a single hydrological year (2023–2024) to quantify global river storage change is its most critical weakness. An anomalous year, heavily influenced by a historic drought in the Amazon, cannot represent the long-term mean or range of variability for global rivers. This makes it difficult for readers to determine whether the significant discrepancy between SWOT observations and model estimates is due to an underestimation by SWOT, an overestimation by previous models, or simply the effect of this single extreme event. text: (a) The reliability of the SWOT product at a global scale is not fully assessed: This is the first global-scale scientific analysis using the SWOT L2 river product. Its performance in estimating river water level and width, particularly its ability to capture seasonal variability, requires a thorough global validation. The authors are encouraged to perform cross-validation using data from traditional altimetry missions with longer time series (e.g., Jason, Sentinel series) for a selection of representative reaches to assess WSE reliability. Furthermore, the accuracy of SWOT-derived width could be validated against high- resolution Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. This would also help quantify the potential error introduced by SWOT's effective 28-day revisit period in capturing flood processes, especially flood peaks.

(1) In the Abstract (e.g., around Line 19), the authors should mention the scope of the river objects studied. text: **Recommendation:** *Accept* The manuscript "Advancing operational global aerosol forecasting with artificial intelligence" details the development of a new class of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) model which incorporates speciated aerosol mass burdens and column-integrated optical properties as state components / channels. Very few works have tackled this problem (especially in the context of building a model suitable for transition to operations), most notably Sleeman et al. (2023, 2025).

cluster: Concern resolution, code, publication readiness, and reproducibility
text: The new model, AI-GAMFS, is trained on NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis dataset and is designed in such a way that it can consume real-time, operational outputs from the NASA GEOS-FP system to initialize forecasts. For this work, the authors actually generate four models, trained for different lead-times (3-, 6-, 9-, and 12- hour) and use a "relay forecasting" technique involving a greedy algorithm to choose the roll-out strategy that uses the fewest number of model inference steps; this is very similar to the "hierarchical" strategy of the Pangu-Weather model by Bi et al. (2022). The model itself uses a relatively simply architecture involving encoder/decoder steps bracketing a convolutional UNet implementing Vision Transformers at the bottleneck.

cluster: Machine learning, model performance, and generalization
text: In multiple comparisons with both global and regional air quality modeling systems spanning a combination of large-scale analysis and case studies, the AI-GAMFS model generally outperforms all existing physics-based models. This includes the most commonly used operational, global aerosol/air quality forecast system, the Copernicus Atmospheric Monitoring Service (CAMS). Performance evaluations and comparisons follow well-established patterns in the broader MLWP literature, and the inclusion of multiple case studies strengthens the authors argument about the generalization of model skill to specific, high- impact events. Inclusion of comparison to AERONET in situ observations versus multiple models further adds to the robustness of the analysis.

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: In its current form, the manuscript is very high quality and requires little if any adjustments prior to publication. Therefore, I recommend accepting the manuscript in its current form. However, I do list below several areas where further discussion or additions to the manuscript could provide further improvements.

text: The article does not discuss temporal drift or trends in the background aerosol burdens in the MERRA-2 dataset. This really leads to three impacts in the manuscript. First, the authors do not discuss what (if any) normalization is applied to the input channels. Any such normalization would likely drift over time as regional AOD shifts due to global policies regarding aerosol and pollutant emissions. Second, the authors do not include a yearly temporal embedding - but any background trend in aerosol burdens within MERRA-2 would likely encode this information. Finally, the generalization / performance of the model is questionable if the drift in the inpur states isn't accounted for somehow.

text: 2. They should also clearly discuss any normalization applied to the data prior to model training, or justify why no normalization was performed. Finally, if possible, the authors should look at the impact of temporal sequencing in their model training. A simple way to do this could be to perform a stratified cross-validation, leaving out one or more years at a time. For instance, they could operate in 7 6-year sequences of the dataset, leaving out one year from the 6-year sequence for validation and then training on all the available data from the remaining 6 sequences. This would provide some indication of how well (or not) the model captures long-term drift in the input.

text: The authors do a commendable job in comparing the impact of different relay forecasting strategies, but there is little discussion of any other hyper-parameters within the modeling framework. Is the model sensitive to the choice of the size of the cube embedding latent space? The number of ViT layers in the bottleneck or the number of attention heads in each layer? Some details of ablation studies exploring the impact of these choices on high-level global model performance would be illustrative for the readers. The model itself is very large - as large or larger than many state-of-the-art MLWP models (for example, the recent MLWP model by Google DeepMind is 180M parameters (Alet et al., 2025)) and while this doesn't seem to be a barrier to operationalization as it runs on an L40 GPU, it still begs fundamental question about how large of a model is actually necessary to solve this composition forecasting task.

text: This study developed an artificial-intelligence-based approach for faster operational forecast of meteorological fields and aerosol abundance. They trained their model based on 42-year archive of NASA MERRA2 output from 1980-2021, and demonstrated better coherence with MERRA2 data testing in year of 2022 and validation in year of 2023 compared to other physics-based forecasting models of CAMS and GEOS-FP, and against other regional models such as for mineral dust simulations over East Asia. text: L35 = line 35 in the manuscript etc. A. Summary of the key results This paper is about an interesting and novel global analysis of night lights, at a high temporal resolution. The core method, to identify both abrupt and gradual NTL changes, is rational and tested. The main interesting element of the manuscript is the focus on the “bidirectional dynamism”, the fact that with NTL the seasonality of urban areas can be captured as well as the impact of several ephemeral and ad hoc events (natural and anthropogenic disasters, pandemics, conflicts etc). NTL are uniquely correlated with socioeconomic activity and urban areas are characterized by constant shifting patterns of activity, even within the same day (e.g. commuting). Classic (day) optical remote sensing can not capture these trends. NTL fill this gap. The paper clearly shows that. B. Originality and significance: if not novel, please include reference The use of daily NTL data on a global scale is novel and significant. The exploitation of NTL fluctuations to describe development trends is original. C. In several instances, throughout the text, it is almost implied that NTL temporal resolution moved from annual to daily, in one step. But in fact, the temporal NTL resolution was initially annual (DMSP/OLS), then it became monthly (VIIRS available since 2012) and more recently it became daily (black marble). The monthly data needs to receive more attention in the manuscript, because it is already available for several years, and solve the seasonality problem for many applications that do not need the daily resolution. Monthly data is a good basis for most analysis within the year, accounting for phenology etc. And several such applications have appeared using monthly data to examine virus spread, population seasonality etc. The clear acknowledgment of the monthly VIIRS data will also help the authors to better focus on the benefit of the daily data. What can daily data do that monthly can not? Also note, that monthly averages are in fact used in some parts of the manuscript (L391, L637-642). claim_target: global generalization, figure evidence, table evidence
cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: This paper presents a first global atlas of observed tidal rivers, based on SWOT measurements. It links to a wonderful interactive web visualization of the identified rivers and associated metrics including tidal extent, amplitude, probability, and number of observations per node. Using the dataset, the authors examine the relationship between river characteristics and their tidal extent. This paper provides a world-first resource, and as such, an important and original contribution worthy of publication. Mapping the tidal characteristics of rivers globally, including regions remote or inaccessible, provides a rich resource for scientific exploration and discovery, and we expect it to be of interest to a wide-ranging readership. The paper is clearly written and well-presented (with a caveat regarding figures 3 and 4, see below). However, before it can be published, the authors should present a more detailed examination of the error budget. Second, the paper should provide more scientific insight – either directly or in the discussion of how the dataset can be utilized. Finally, the visualization of the data is uneven and should be improved upon to be suitable for a Nature publication.

text: UTide is a robust analysis tool, well-suited for this kind of global survey; however, did you investigate using the NS_TIDE package for rivers where there is adequate discharge data to compare to results for UTide? (Matte et al. 2013, https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-12-00016.1) NS_TIDE is "adapted to the study of nonstationary signals, in this case, river tides. It builds the nonstationary forcing directly into the tidal basis functions. It is implemented by modification of T_TIDE; however, certain concepts, particularly the meaning of a constituent and the Rayleigh criterion, are redefined to account for the smearing effects on the tidal spectral lines by nontidal energy." If UTide tidal amplitudes are similar to NS_TIDE for well-constrained rivers, it would bolster global results for rivers where there are insufficient or non-existent discharge records. If there is substantial disagreement, this could help indicate how much error is introduced by neglecting the interaction of tides and river discharge.

cluster: Remote-sensing context, citation positioning, and prior work
text: The novelty of this manuscript is the usage of the SWOT altimetry mission and the extension to the downstream part of rivers. The authors only estimate the diurnal O1 and semi-diurnal M2 tidal constituents, as they state the current SWOT record is too short. They use an high level product called “RiverSP” that provides preprocessed water surface levels spaced around 200 m. The estimation of tides is automatized in order to create a global atlas of tides within rivers. Validation of SWOT-derived tides is made using ground truth at 663 sites. Three rivers (Gironde, Seine, and Elbe) are analyzed in detail. Some other big rivers (Hudson, Amazon, Yangtze) are also highlighted.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: SWOT is essentially a SAR system looking down at very low incidence angles. It uses the interferometry principle to estimate surface level changes. The KaRIn instrument permits to acquire Single‐Look‐ Complex images. Then a product called “PIXC” is derived that is the input for the “RiverSP” product used here. The algorithm to estimate surface level elevations is extremely complex. There is a static mask of prior water probability used during processing that informs where water might be expected. It is not perfect for two reasons: a) it cannot be perfect as water is dynamic; b) the transformation of ground coordinates to slant-plane coordinates is also uncertain and depends on the water height itself. Therefore, there is an impact in determining if a pixel is water or land or mixed.

cluster: Concern resolution, code, publication readiness, and reproducibility
text: The power of echoes is also important in the classification. The document titled “SWOT Science Data Products User Handbook (JPL D-109532, Revision A, March 2025) states that “water detection for HR data over land assumes that water is brighter than the surrounding land”. An example of the Connecticut River is provided (page 169). If the water is not much more reflective than land, it may not be detected as water in the KaRIn ground processing. This would cause errors.

text: Other two important issues are: a) the frequent presence of smooth waters (known in SAR domain as dark waters) that reflect very little radar energy at the KaRIn off-nadir incidence angles; b) the brightness of side lobes (called specular ringing). There are other caveats (e.g., layover, phase unwrapping, etc.). Several quality flags are provided in the products and must to be carefully scrutinized.

But also data flagged ”good” might be “bad”. This is why a data analyses is necessary. SWOT is certainly an intriguing satellite mission, but the complex processing calls for a severe data screening and I don’t see any analyses in the paper.

text: Also, the paper has major focus on a data set and some statistics. The reader would expect to see some new scientific insights from tidal fields in the rivers (e.g., tidal bore phenomena; tidal field propagation velocity; relationship with drought/flooding extreme events; salinity intrusions, etc.). But not a speculative statement like “Interestingly, within our global assessment, more than half of the investigated rivers (54.36%) exhibit e.g. upstream amplification similar to the Elbe”. If tides amplify as they travel upstream river it depends on local conditions. For instance I have doubt this happens e.g. if the river mouth is wide and open to the sea without much constriction or e.g. if there is high discharge. Anyway, the above statement must to be proved. A global atlas of tides from space in coastal rivers is certainly of interest to a wide audience, however, the analyses need to be rigorous. The reader expects that 1) SWOT observations are scrutinized in depth before estimating tides; 2) the tidal estimates are explained keeping in mind the relevant physical processes occurring in the selected sites.

cluster: Remote-sensing context, citation positioning, and prior work
text: Validation of SWOT-derived tidal estimates - Reviewer 3 noted that the validation of SWOT-derived tidal estimates is insufficiently addressed. We respectfully take a different view. While SWOT observations are indeed relatively new, a substantial body of work has already been published on their characteristics and performance. The manuscript relies on the best-available SWOT products and builds on prior validation efforts documented in the literature. In our assessment, this constitutes a reasonable and well-justified methodological foundation.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: Uncertainty of tidal amplitude estimates versus WSE errors - Reviewer 3 expressed skepticism regarding tidal amplitude errors of only a few centimeters, given reported water surface elevation (WSE) uncertainties on the order of 10–18 cm (68th percentile). We believe this concern arises from a comparison of quantities that are not directly equivalent. Tidal amplitudes are derived through harmonic analysis applied to extended WSE time series, and it is therefore expected that the uncertainty of fitted parameters can be substantially lower than that of individual observations. In our view, this difference does not indicate a methodological flaw.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: Comparability with tide gauge observations - Reviewer 3 suggested that hourly-sampled tide gauge data may not capture the same dynamics as SWOT observations. However, the manuscript focuses on tidal amplitudes and phases derived from harmonic analysis of complete time series, rather than on point-by-point WSE comparisons. Tides have periods of several hours. Therefore, the time sampling interval only matters to correctly identify alias frequencies, but does not impact the comparability of the derived amplitudes.

text: Concerns related to SAR imaging geometry and dark water - Reviewer 3 raised the concern that water appears dark in a typical SAR imaging geometry, from which they derived the need for further data analysis / case studies. All results derived from the SWOT data are doubted hereafter. However, in contrast to typical SAR imaging systems like Sentinel-1, the looking angle of SWOT's radar antennae is tuned to 1-4 degrees (instead of ~30 degrees) in order to observe bright reflections from water instead. The authors demonstrate this in an illustrative plot, and using the statistics of the dark water flag, which is native to the data products. Brightness (and related SNR) can easily be assessed through the observations themselves, so that only little doubt can remain regarding the correctness of, e.g., the dark water flag. The authors defend their point well, by hinting to the relevant literature and documentation. This near-nadir geometry is one of the features that makes SWOT observations unique, so the point that the reviewer made here was completely unsubstantiated.

text: Cui et al. present an interesting study examining the relationship between rainfall and deforestation across the Amazon Basin using novel methods of water vapor tracking and weighted forest cover. While the topic is of broad interest and the approach is potentially innovative, the manuscript suffers from critical flaws in structure, logic, and clarity, preventing me from recommending it for publication in Nature Communications. Below are my major and minor comments:

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: 1. Disconnection between title, introduction, and results. The manuscript lacks cohesion. The title refers to deforestation’s impact on rainfall, the introduction centers around “Amazon rainforest dieback,” while the results focus on rainfall changes and attribution. These elements are poorly organized and not conceptually aligned.

cluster: Amazon, forest cover, land-use pressure, and forest resilience
text: 2. Overemphasis on Amazon dieback: Although Amazon dieback is an important issue, it is not the central topic of this paper. The introduction devotes considerable space to it, with little mention of vegetation–rainfall feedback or deforestation impacts on precipitation. This misalignment continues in the implications section. While dieback may be a consequence, it should not dominate the narrative.

cluster: River, water storage, sediment, tidal, and hydraulic interpretation
text: 3. Causal logic is flawed: The study investigates rainfall changes and attributes them to various factors, identifying deforestation as a potential driver. However, it incorrectly reverses this conclusion to claim that deforestation drives rainfall changes without robust causal evidence. Moreover, the paper does not even introduce or describe the deforestation dataset

cluster: Remote-sensing context, citation positioning, and prior work
text: 4. Misplaced novelty: The true novelty lies in the use of a new water vapor tracking method and the weighted forest cover metric to assess deforestation's impact on recycled and total rainfall — not in addressing the Amazon dieback issue, which the authors discuss extensively and disproportionately.

text: 5. Misrepresentation of prior literature and conceptual confusion: L12–13: The claim that few studies focus on deforestation’s impact on rainfall is misleading. This, along with other imprecise language, suggests a limited understanding of vegetation–climate feedback and a lack of sufficient background review on this key issue.

The method used to derive recycled precipitation is disconnected from deforestation, yet the second part of the manuscript makes a subjective determination that the results are induced by deforestation based on “visual correlations”. cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: 2. High methodological risk in projecting a weak historical linkage linearly into the future. The manuscript extrapolates a very weak historical relationship between deforestation and precipitation directly into future climate scenarios using a linear approach. This practice poses significant scientific risks and undermines the credibility of the projections.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: 3. Lack of clear distinction between total terrestrial moisture and Amazonian-sourced moisture. The manuscript does not clearly differentiate between “total terrestrial moisture” and “Amazonian-sourced moisture.” Given the stated research aims and study design, the analysis should explicitly tag and track Amazonian-sourced moisture, rather than using the broader “terrestrial moisture” metric. This misuse creates logical inconsistencies and may fundamentally alter the interpretation of the results. For example, by tagging all land grids, the calculated recycled precipitation is artificially elevated, because it includes contributions from land areas outside the Amazon basin. This additional portion has no connection to the Amazonian moisture, deforestation, and future deforestation, yet the authors interpret and present it as “Amazonian-sourced moisture” and use them for attribution explanation and future projection thereby conflating two distinct concepts. text: The study “Thermodynamic amplification of extreme Greenland Ice Sheet melt events attributable to anthropogenic climate change” aims to attribute the 10 most extreme Greenland ice sheet melting events from 1950 to 2023 by decomposing the relative contributions of thermodynamic versus dynamic drivers. The idea is to address the question: how much of the intensification of extreme melt is due to direct surface warming v/s changes in atmospheric circulation patterns that favour melt. Furthermore, the authors use CMIP5/CMIP6 climate models to project the future intensification of extreme melt events under high-emission scenarios (RCP8.5, SSP5-8.5) to 2100, with a particular focus on identifying regional hotspots, especially in northwest and northern Greenland, where the risk of extreme melt accelerates most. I think the study is thorough and well written in general. The two reviewers’ have rightly pointed out a few shortcomings and improvements. My comments to the authors’ response to the original reviews is appended below. text: I believe that the authors have made improvements, like clarifying the title to emphasize thermodynamic amplification and softening language in the abstract. However, it appears that they have perhaps sidestepped the reviewer's core concern rather than addressing it. The reviewer's point was not that flow analogue methods are invalid, but rather the claim "attribution to anthropogenic climate change" without performing the model-based attribution (likelihood in all-forcing vs. natural-only scenarios) that such claims require. The authors’ response instead defends their method by citing IPCC AR6, which is not the point here as showing that analogue methods are established science does not prove they constitute formal anthropogenic attribution. I understand that adding a new analysis is tedious, but perhaps the authors may explicitly state (whereever they may need to) that this is conditional attribution and does not include model-based likelihood comparison.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: This manuscript presents a technically impressive and conceptually important advance in the study of urban spatial disparities. By mapping the function of 110 million individual buildings across 109 Chinese cities using 1-meter multi-modal satellite imagery, the authors produce the first building-level, nationwide dataset of urban building functions. The reported accuracy, with overall accuracy of 84%, is satisfactory for a national-scale mapping task. Moreover, upon examining their code repository and raw data, the authors have made their workflow reproducible and transparent. This is particularly important because the methodological framework could be transferable beyond China.

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: Leveraging this self-produced dataset, the authors assess spatial disparities across three dimensions: urbanization intensity, facility accessibility, and infrastructure sufficiency. The creation of this high-resolution (1-meter), building-level product enables the study to reveal nuances that previous research, with coarser data, might have missed. For example, the study provides novel insights into how spatial disparities manifest across city tiers, regions, and intra-city zones, highlighting the uneven distribution of public services, the unexpected housing equality in mid-tier cities, and the infrastructure strain in rapidly growing southern cities. The authors also attempt to link these spatial disparities to long-term development policies (e.g., Third-Front Movement, Northeast Revitalization), offering historical and policy context. These findings also offer some practical insights for understanding urban development in China, and bring interest to researches in related fields.

text: In the revised statement the “high SIF emission reflects efficient photochemical activity” is partially misleading. SIF intensity does not directly increase with photosynthetic efficiency. When photochemical efficiency is high, a larger fraction of absorbed light is used for photochemistry, leaving less energy available for fluorescence and heat dissipation. Therefore, SIF yield tends to decrease when photochemistry is most efficient, even though total SIF emission may still appear high under strong illumination because of increased light absorption. So, high SIF emission generally indicates active photosynthesis and high light use, but not necessarily high efficiency. (Remarks on code availability)

text: This is a very interesting, thorough and original paper which uses a combination of high-resolution remote sensing and machine learning to estimate global losses and gains to saltmarsh carbon pools via changes to marsh extent and surface SOC density. The combination of techniques, with field validation, gives strong results which are well justified within the context of other literature. The figures are very clear and well-presented. The authors highlight the importance of conserving established marshes with high surface SOC density, as well as restoring new saltmarsh sites, which is an important finding as restoration efforts increase, and offers a timely and insightful contribution to the field. I have three main feedback points:

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: 1) The study chooses to use the surface 0-20cm for SOC estimates, which is well justified and implicitly incorporates differences in SOC density between older and newly deposited sediments. However, the estimates for SOC gains/losses rely upon changes to this surface SOC density and changes to saltmarsh lateral extent, but do not incorporate potential vertical changes (accretion, vertical erosion) which may also play a substantial role. While it is likely sufficient to use surface stocks in the analysis, the potential for changes to total SOC stocks via vertical extent changes should be further discussed

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: 2) The use of SOC density to calculate carbon stocks does not account for the contribution of autochthonous carbon (directly stored by the marsh) and allochthonous carbon (imported to the marsh). While this is fine for stock estimates, it does mean that gains and losses may include carbon which might have been stored anyway by another system – e.g. if the carbon was stored, for example, by a seagrass system but imported to the marsh, the gain in marsh area may not necessarily result in ‘additional’ carbon being stored. The discussion could be expanded to discuss different carbon sources and to caveat the limitations in gain/loss estimates.

cluster: River, water storage, sediment, tidal, and hydraulic interpretation
text: 3) It would be good to be consistent with the terminology used to describe carbon sequestration, accumulation, storage and burial throughout the manuscript. Sequestration typically refers to the direct uptake via vegetation within the marsh itself, whereas accumulation can include carbon stored by the marsh via trapping of imported sediment. These could be defined earlier in the manuscript and a more consistency given to where each is used.

Using higher-quality satellite data like Sentinel-2 can provide more detailed information, and carefully adding GEDI LiDAR data can help confirm canopy height measurements, even though there are some issues with grasslands. text: This is a welcome and important contribution and I unreservedly recommend publication. The potential impact of sea-level rise on coastal wetlands has been a major theme of research in recent years, and good progress has been made understanding the tipping points associated with mangrove and tidal marsh survival. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of tidal marsh and mangrove habitat change at high temporal and spatial resolution for the conterminous USA. The United States is a fascinating case study, given strong regional differences in the rate of sea-level rise and exposure to extreme storms. The results provide perhaps the first detailed continental-scale assessment of the relative contributions of sea-level rise, extreme storms and anthropogenic stressors in shaping the extent of these important wetlands. The finding that sea-level rise is historically the dominant driver, but that extreme storms are increasing in their relative contribution is a very important finding. As the authors argue in their concluding statements, the two drivers are increasingly interacting in driving a trend of reduced tidal marsh extent. Mangrove low latitude losses appear offset by poleward expansion for now.

text: Caution for the boreal biome results: for the boreal biome in general fires are forest regeneration events, and do not represent longer-term loss of forest like urban expansion or conversion to agriculture. Fires there are complex in shape, have unburned islands within the fire perimeter, and generate some increases in edge density, but in many cases those differences will disappear when the forest regenerates. Also the regeneration process is slow compared to temperate forests, so 12 years of observation will not always show the recovery. In addition there is conversion from coniferous to deciduous (birch or aspen) forests in a lot of cases, and those early-successional deciduous boreal forests will have lower values of the indexes calculated here for one to several decades (compared to the pre-fire condition).

text: Yin et al. “Ozone mitigates extended growing season and enhanced vegetation greenness driven by climate change” This study assesses the impact of surface ozone on global vegetation phenology. The findings indicate that ozone delays the start of season (SOS) and advances the end of season (EOS) in highly polluted regions such as the United States, Europe, and China. To some extent, this effect offsets the extension of the growing season driven by global warming. While the study presents novel insights, it has substantial limitations in terms of data, methodology, and mechanistic explanations.

The study primarily employs linear correlations, which are inadequate for capturing nonlinear relationships between variables and fail to account for collinearity among factors. Although partial correlation analysis was used, collinearity issues cannot be entirely eliminated. Additionally, in future projections, the study assumes five future scenarios with fixed ozone concentration change rates. text: Third, the conclusions are not reliable. The study relies on correlation analysis, yet the correlation coefficients between phenological parameters and both temperature and ozone are very low. For example, correlation coefficients between AOT40 and SOS were only 0.15 ± 0.04 in the U.S., 0.06 ± 0.02 in Europe, and 0.10 ± 0.03 in China (Lines 149-150). Spatial distribution maps of Fig. 3a reveal a highly scattered response in China, lacking a clear and significant pattern. Moreover, the study claims that ozone leads to a decline in EVImax (Fig. 3e). However, in recent years, ozone concentration in China has been increasing (Li et al., 2020), while EVImax and vegetation greenness have also shown a significant upward trend (Chen et al., 2019). text: Plant functional traits are essential to ecosystem functioning and Earth system processes. However, global-scale trait data remain limited due to the sparse and uneven coverage of field-based surveys. This study proposes a multi-resolution framework that integrates remote sensing data, global crowd-sourced biodiversity records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), and trait information from the TRY database to generate global maps of community-weighted means (CWMs) for plant functional traits at a spatial resolution of 1 km. Building upon the foundational work of Moreno- Martínez et al. (2018) and Dechant et al. (2024), the proposed methodology addresses spatial biases stemming from the uneven geographic distribution of GBIF records by incorporating remotely sensed distributions of plant functional types (PFTs). This integration enhances both the representativeness and ecological interpretability of trait estimates.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: In addition to CWMs, the study quantifies statistical moments—including standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis—to characterize trait distributions, explicitly accounting for PFT variability and compositional uniformity, using supplementary data from the sPlotOpen database. PFT fractions are derived from a downscaled 500-meter version of the MODIS land cover product (MCD12Q1, Land Cover Type 5: Annual Plant Functional Types classification). Overall, this study introduces a novel approach to global trait mapping that aims to improve both the spatial resolution and ecological relevance of key plant functional traits, including specific leaf area (SLA), leaf nitrogen concentration (LNC), and leaf phosphorus concentration (LPC). This study proposes an innovative framework that integrates remote sensing and biodiversity data to produce global plant trait maps. However, several concerns outlined below require clarification.

Cross Scales and Spatial Bias The integration of heterogeneous datasets—point-based species occurrence records (GBIF), species-level trait data (TRY), 500 m MODIS imagery, and 30 m Landsat data—introduces scale mismatches that may result in information loss or distortion. Aggregating finer-resolution data into a 1 km grid could exacerbate the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP), potentially smoothing out critical spatial heterogeneity. Furthermore, despite weighting schemes to correct for spatial bias in GBIF data, residual effects likely remain. These limitations should be discussed in greater depth. 3.Scale Dependency and Spatial Autocorrelation Ecological processes are inherently scale-dependent, and spatial autocorrelation is often pronounced across ecological gradients. Although the use of PFT fractions helps mitigate sampling bias and spatial heterogeneity, the potential impact of spatial autocorrelation and neighborhood effects on trait estimates—especially in data-poor or ecologically heterogeneous areas—should be discussed. Additionally, uncertainties arising from MODIS downscaling and Landsat-based classification may propagate through the trait-weighting process. Providing uncertainty maps for trait estimates would be beneficial.

text: The article “Leveraging Remote Sensing and Crowd-Sourced Biodiversity Data for Enhanced Plant Functional Trait Mapping” presents a new approach to creating maps of three crucial leaf traits at global scale. The topic is of high importance for global change studies, but also a very challenging one - many trait maps have been published to date, and few of them are reliable. The novelty of the study lies in estimating species abundance data from occurrence data in a new way as well as the extension of the mapping to summary statistics beyond mean trait values. I found the paper to be well written, with an excellent introduction that concisely lays out the challenge. I also found the methodological innovations in terms of abundance estimation interesting and worthy of further exploration. And, ultimately, it would be an excellent addition to have maps of variance and skew.

cluster: Spatial data, resolution, and product coverage
text: 1. Circularities in validation: First, the validation is presented as independent from the map generation, but as far as I understand, this is not true. The landcover / PFT product is used to produce the 1 km maps, and then the same landcover / PFT product is used to adjust the validation plots to a “top-of-canopy weighted mean” (TWM). I do not have a full understanding of how the PFT product was applied in both cases - and I am happy to be corrected by the authors -, but I doubt that the TWM-corrected plots provide a truly independent validation if the same product is involved in both cases. If only the direct data from the validation database are used (CWMs), the maps’ predictive power (on log-scales, cf. point 4 below) falls to R2 ~ 0.1 for two traits, and R2 ~ 0.3 for the third trait, which is hardly a strong prediction. For broadly reliable maps, R2 values around 0.7-0.8 are just about ok, but not great, but R2 values in the range of 0.1-0.3 are highly problematic.

text: I also found the reporting of errors to be problematic. First, R2 is the most common metric to assess model performance and should be reported instead of unsquared correlations. Second, all traits are mapped on log-scales. Alternative R2 values (on backtransformed scales) should be provided, and crucially, mean errors and RMSEs should be interpreted multiplicatively. An RMSE of 0.36 on logscale for SLA roughly means that the errors in the backtransformed SLA are given through multiplication with error terms equal to exp(N(0,0.36)). Using the software R to calculate quantile(exp(rnorm(100000,0,0.36)),probs = c(0.025,0.975)), we obtain a 95% range of 0.5 and 2, so predictions can be off by as much as a factor of 2, or a 50% error downwards, and a 100% error upwards.

text: The validation with actual CWM values from field plots shows very low predictive power (R2 of 0.10-0.27 on logscales, R2 = 0.11-0.25 on original scales). The predictive power declines even further when aggregated at 0.5 degree scale (R2 of 0.14- 0.19). I agree with the authors that very high R2 values are unrealistic given the scale mismatches and the broad ecological context, but R2 values < 0.3 at original spatial scales and < 0.2 at coarser scales (0.5 degree) are far from moderate even by ecological standards and insufficient to create reliable maps. The issue is compounded by the fact that tropical forests, likely the hardest to map, are underrepresented in the sPlotOpen collection, and that a longitude-latitude grid is used (instead of area-preserving CRS). Together these collections would provide systematic samples of top-of-canopy plants/trees across a wide geographic and environmental range. Often these tree inventories are accompanied by systematic sampling of shrubs and herb layers in subplots. This would be the perfect resource to test trait maps, and it would also allow to create TWMs directly from the field data, removing the circularity issue. Together these inventories likely also cover a much larger area than sPlotOpen. I agree with the authors that the situation is much more difficult in the tropics, where data are often accessible only through closed networks, but there is still a substantial amount of open plot data that have been recently released, for example, through ForestGEO, and there are open legacy collections such as RADAMBRASIL which would allow the authors to put

cluster: Long-term time series, climate variability, and trend interpretation
text: together a nice test data set. Furthermore, while I agree in principle that noise from small plot data could inflate the errors, I am doubtful that this is the main reason for the low R2. Plot noise from scale mismatches would be expected to average out at coarser scales, e.g., at 0.5 degree. The fact that R2 decreases when aggregating plot data in 0.5 degree grid cells, indicates to me that noise is not the primary cause of low R2, but rather systematic mapping errors. Alternatively, it is also possible that the validation at the original scale is geographically biased. I.e., the sPlotOpen data may be concentrated in a few 0.5 degree grid cells and thus inflate performance at the original scale through spatial autocorrelation, which is then reduced at coarser scales. A good way of testing this would be to randomly select one plot from each 0.5 degree grid cell, test the predictive power of the maps, and then repeat this, for example 1000x. If there was no autocorrelation bias in the original validation, then this approach should not lead to a decrease in predictive power.

text: This study leverages multi-source satellite retrievals (OCO-2, XCO₂) and a biogeochemical model (GCASv2) to dissect the drivers behind the record-breaking atmospheric CO₂ growth rate (CGR) observed in 2024. Its central conclusion is that compound hot-and-humid extremes markedly intensify total ecosystem respiration (TER), thereby weakening the terrestrial carbon sink. These findings are valuable for understanding carbon-cycle–climate feedbacks. Nevertheless, several critical issues merit fuller consideration: 1.The paper attributes the abrupt 2024 decline in the land carbon sink mainly to a sharp rise in TER, positing that (i) compound hot–dry extremes suppress GPP and (ii) compound hot–wet extremes enhance TER (Lines 317-320). This is an interesting hypothesis, but the satellite and carbon-assimilation framework alone cannot elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms. Controlled experiments or long-term eddy-covariance flux datasets are needed to strengthen the argument—for example, to partition autotrophic versus heterotrophic respiration contributions. 2.Many studies report a nonlinear temperature response of ecosystem respiration, with rates leveling off beyond a critical

Beyond climatic and GPP effects, quantifying the contribution of LUCC to TER shifts would further solidify the findings. 4.While compound hot–wet extremes are deemed a key driver of elevated TER, the temperature and moisture thresholds at which ecosystems face a net carbon-sink loss remain unclear. Defining these thresholds is vital for fine-tuning ecosystem carbon management strategies. 5.TER is derived from multiple data streams (Line 577), and its accuracy hinges on upstream data quality. text: In this manuscript, the authors report an analysis of chemistry of the plume of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha’apai (HTHH) eruption of January 2016, which was emitted into the stratosphere. Using data from satellite observations, principally TROPOMI, high amounts of HCHO are shown to be present in two clouds this stratospheric plume. The peak HCHO concentration is determined to be the highest ever observed within the stratosphere.

The authors argue is evidence of continual HCHO formation from volcanogenic methane. Methane is theorised to have been oxidised by chlorine radicals. The authors argue that substantial continuous chlorine radical production is required to explain the observations, which is theorised to be produced by iron photochemistry.

text: Bromine chemistry is dismissed as a potential mechanism here, on the basis that observed BrO is too low. There is evidence that the plume from the bromine-rich part of the eruption was separate from this plume that is the focus of this study. I would however still want to see greater discussion of this mechanism before it is dismissed. While the BrO content of this part of the plume is lower, this does not fully evidence that the reactive bromine content of this part of the plume is effectively nil. Is the bromine content of this part of the plume constrained significantly by observations to consider its impacts to be negligible? The reference here to von Glasow (2010) is not adequate, that paper considers principally bromine chemistry of passively degassing plumes within the troposphere, and the field has advanced significantly since 2010. For example, Narivelo et al. (2023) modelled bromine cycling releasing significant reactive chlorine from chloride-containing aerosol.

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: The authors aim to improve the integration of coastal subsidence with sea-level change and provide a global assessment that integrates the best-available datasets on VLM (or assumed VLM) through a hierarchical workflow to arrive to an integrated VLM dataset. This is then compared to (linear) sea level change data and used to compute the amount of (average) relative sea-level rise people living along the worlds coasts are experiencing. This work is in itself highly relevant and may become a showcase on how to integrate various VLM data. While in general the authors take great care to discuss the results and limitations of the study (and also provide already a level of error propagation in the results), there are several aspects in the study which need to be considered to make the work more robust and to have the conclusions of the study rightfully underpinned. Several of the current workflow and data processing decisions may lead to an overestimation of VLM attribution to population, while at the same time potentially underestimating SLC. These issues are mendable and when properly dealt with this paper deserves publication at a level of Nature Comms, as I expect this paper to become influential

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: 1) In their MS the authors directly infer VLM from InSAR. This is a common practice in which InSAR-estimated elevation change between satellite passes is directly interpreted as VLM, while it is an estimate of reflector distance difference (may or may not be caused by a motion). Assuming InSAR-estimated rates as VLM is an assumption at several levels (e.g. the observed difference in reflector distance is caused by VLM), but also that the observed InSAR values (which also go through a number of processing and post processing steps) indeed provide an estimate of VLM. This study is not processing InSAR but uses existing InSAR datasets so there is no first-handed processing, however for the clarity and robustness of the workflow, clearly considering the involved assumption – and their potential impacts on the results of the this study – are of importance in this manuscript. Moreover as I expect this to be an exemplar study which will be followed by others in the future – this is the moment to set the bar.

text: In the InSAR Deltas dataset section the interpolation methods is described. Here the authors choose to use the spatial average, instead of the median. By following this practice, assumably also for the other InSAR datasets, the workflow itself has the tendency to overestimate the average experienced VLM per bulk population number. Especially for areas which experience high rates and high spatial variability in subsidence rates (e.g. deltas, cities with high differential subsidence) applying a spatial average is likely skewing the results towards higher rates for the entire segment (see e.g. Thieblémont et al., 2024). Why not use the median instead to avoid this skewing effect and potential overprediction of subsidence for an entire segment? To investigate the impact of this potential skewing effect, please provide a comparison using a median interpolation method as well (for the delta InSAR but also the other InSAR datasets). As such the authors will be able to quantify the potential spatial ‘over-prediction’ of higher subsidence for larger areas due to the skewing effect which may caused by very local phenomena (e.g. a certain part of a city may sink very fast, e.g. northern harbour in Jakarta, which then

text: The paper presents a synthesis of globally available constraints on vertical land motion and sea surface elevation to provide a population-weighted measure of impact from relative sea level rise, focusing especially on major cities. The contributing datasets include InSAR, GNSS, tide gauges, altimetry and GIA models and sea surface satellite altimetry. The focus is on how the imaged relative sea level change impacts the human population. It will probably get some attention since sea level rise is of such high concern among the slow environmental risks facing society today. The paper is generally well written and seems to fit the appearance of articles published in Nature Communications in terms of length, voice, graphic quality,

The title is catchy, and it is interesting that the coastal human population tends to be concentrated in areas where VLM sign is on balance subsidence and are low lying. text: The authors present a highly innovative project that leverages high-frequency satellite imagery to characterize and measure local market activity in East Africa. In contexts where traditional data on economic activity are scarce, their approach offers a novel and valuable contribution to the literature on unconventional data sources. The manuscript is well-structured and clearly written, with a detailed methodology and compelling new results. To further strengthen the paper, I recommend a more thorough comparison of their findings with existing data sources and a deeper discussion of the external validity and reproducibility of their methods in diverse settings. Below, I provide specific comments on the data, model, and methodology.

claim_target: figure evidence, table evidence, methodological support

Clarity and Accessibility of the Methodology The methodology, particularly in the section “Detecting and Tracking Marketplaces,” is technically rigorous but dense, which may hinder readability for non-specialist audiences. To improve accessibility, I suggest either simplifying the main text and relocating more technical details to a dedicated appendix or retaining the current section but supplementing it with a concise summary in the form of a figure or table.

External Validity and Scalability While Ethiopia serves as an excellent case study, the discussion on external validity could be expanded to address the global prevalence of periodic markets and the potential for this method to be applied in other contexts, such as pastoralist regions or urban informal markets. Additionally, it could also discuss the adaptability of the methodology to various geographic and socioeconomic settings, including its limitations and the requirements for successful implementation.

text: 4. Market Monitoring During Humanitarian Crises The section on market monitoring during the Tigray conflict is informative but raises questions about the comprehensiveness of the analysis. Economic activity may have shifted to forms not observable via satellite imagery, potentially biasing the estimates. I suggest clarifying the objectives of this section and explicitly acknowledging the limitations of satellite-based observations in crisis settings. For instance, economic activities could have taken another form that is unobservable when using satellite imagery, which might make the authors’ estimates represent an upper bound.

cluster: Methods, results, discussion structure, and explanatory clarity
text: Validation: The authors used the entire validation set to both set the threshold and evaluate performance metrics. The threshold was chosen to maximize the performance metrics that were reported. These metrics are thus not independent from the selection mechanism. I suggest splitting the validation data into a validation and test set, where the threshold is set based on the validation data and the metrics reported on the test data.

text: Map: There is no rigorous evaluation of the Ethiopia market map. I suggest following best practices from [1] and/or [2] to conduct an unbiased accuracy assessment of the map. The sample design could use a stratified sample using strata such as the detected market locations, the Sentinel-2 candidate locations (likely areas of omission), the population map (likely areas of omission), and the non-market detection areas. This assumes humans can identify whether a market is present or not, which I think is a correct assumption based on the error analysis discussed in the paper.

text: 1. I think the paper still over-emphasizes the potential value of this new measure for applications that are never critically evaluated in the manuscript. I reiterate my prior concern: those applications are just speculative, and are not supported by analysis in the paper (i.e., there is no empirical evidence that the measure of market activity would actually improve such policies). I am particularly worried that some of the limitations of the method (e.g., that it misses certain types of markets, does not detect any markets in some regions, etc.) could have disastrous implications if policies (e.g., targeting assistance) were based largely on this new method. I would suggest that these statements be removed, to ensure the reader does not draw potentially irresponsible conclusions. Alternatively, if the authors wish to continue to refer to such applications, the specific use cases should be discussed in more detail, with empirical justification, and with explicit language about the caveats and limitations that are likely to arise in those applications.

text: Interactions and economic development The paper uses HDI to assess the results, categorizing cities into four HDI groups.
